$note: Primary-source research findings for the GRU953 benchmark. Every finding was verified by an independent research agent against the organisation's own current page, read 20 August 2026. This file is hand-curated research input, not generated output -- it is the source, analogous to the four colour direction JSON files: the one place in this domain where a human (here, a research agent under strict sourcing rules) types something in.
method: Eight parallel research agents, each required to cite a primary source read live on the date above, quote the supporting sentence verbatim for any numeric claim, and mark anything unconfirmed as could_not_verify rather than guess.

findings.question: What is the exact master canvas size and shape for iOS/iPadOS/macOS app icons?
findings.claim: For iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, Apple's current HIG specifies a square 1024x1024 px layout canvas, authored as layered artwork, which the system masks into a rounded rectangle. Six appearance variants are listed: default, dark, clear light, clear dark, tinted light, tinted dark.
findings.quoted_line: iOS, iPadOS, macOS | Square | Rounded rectangle (square) | 1024x1024 px | Layered | Default, dark, clear light, clear dark, tinted light, tinted dark
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Is the watchOS app icon canvas 1088x1088 px rather than 1024x1024 px?
findings.claim: Confirmed: watchOS uses a 1088x1088 px square layout canvas (not 1024), layered style, masked by the system into a circle.
findings.quoted_line: watchOS | Square | Circular | 1088x1088 px | Layered | N/A
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What is the visionOS app icon canvas size and shape?
findings.claim: visionOS uses a square 1024x1024 px layout canvas, style 'Layered (3D)', masked by the system into a circle.
findings.quoted_line: visionOS | Square | Circular | 1024x1024 px | Layered (3D) | N/A
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does Apple publish any corner radius, percentage, or squircle value for app icon masking?
findings.claim: No. Apple's current HIG states only that the system's masking matches the curvature of other interface elements and the device bezel; it publishes no numeric radius, percentage, or squircle formula for designers to use, and explicitly tells designers to supply square, unmasked layers and let the system apply the mask.
findings.quoted_line: In iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, icons are square, and the system applies masking to produce rounded corners that precisely match the curvature of other rounded interface elements throughout the system and the bezel of the physical device itself.
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Which platforms mask app icons to a circle rather than a rounded rectangle?
findings.claim: Confirmed: visionOS and watchOS are the two platforms where Apple's system masks the square icon layout into a circle; iOS, iPadOS, and macOS mask to a rounded rectangle, and tvOS masks a rectangular (landscape) layout to a rounded rectangle.
findings.quoted_line: In visionOS and watchOS, icons are square and the system applies circular masking.
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What appearance/layer variants does Icon Composer author?
findings.claim: As of the current (20 Aug 2026) HIG wording, Icon Composer is where a designer authors and annotates three appearance variants directly — default, dark, and mono — not the six-variant 'light/dark/clear/tinted' set. The additional system-facing variants (clear light, clear dark, tinted light, tinted dark) are auto-generated by the system from what's supplied, per the Appearances section on the same page.
findings.quoted_line: In Icon Composer, you define the background layer for your icon, adjust your foreground layer placement, apply visual effects like specular highlights and refraction, annotate for default, dark, and mono appearance variants, test and preview your icon across system versions, and export your icon for use in Xcode.
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What appearance choices does the system offer people for Home Screen icons (as distinct from what Icon Composer authors)?
findings.claim: The system-facing appearance choices people can pick for Home Screen icons are described as default, dark, clear, or tinted (with clear and tinted each having light/dark sub-variants per the specifications table, totalling six named variants) — a different, larger set than the three (default/dark/mono) that Icon Composer has the designer directly annotate.
findings.quoted_line: In iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, people can choose whether their Home Screen app icons are default, dark, clear, or tinted in appearance.
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What does Apple say happens if you supply pre-masked (already rounded) icon layers instead of square unmasked ones?
findings.claim: Apple explicitly warns against pre-masking: supplying layers with their own corner/circle masking already applied harms the specular-highlight lighting effects the system draws and makes the icon's edges look jagged rather than crisp.
findings.quoted_line: Providing layers with pre-defined masking negatively impacts specular highlight effects and makes edges look jagged.
findings.source_title: App icons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does Apple publish any specific contrast ratio for text over a material (e.g. Liquid Glass)?
findings.claim: No. The Materials HIG page gives only qualitative guidance for text-over-material legibility (use vibrant colors, choose thicker materials for more opaque contrast, thinner for context-visibility) with no numeric contrast ratio anywhere on the page. It does not reference WCAG or any ratio at all in the materials context.
findings.quoted_line: Help ensure legibility by using vibrant colors on top of materials. When you use system-defined vibrant colors, you don't need to worry about colors seeming too dark, bright, saturated, or low contrast in different contexts.
findings.source_title: Materials - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Is there any concrete number published on the Materials page relating to contrast for Liquid Glass?
findings.claim: The only concrete numeric value on the Materials page is not a contrast ratio but a recommended dimming-layer opacity: for clear Liquid Glass placed over bright underlying content, Apple suggests a 35%-opacity dark dimming layer to preserve legibility.
findings.quoted_line: If the underlying content is bright, consider adding a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity.
findings.source_title: Materials - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does Apple defer text contrast to platform APIs / WCAG rather than publishing its own ratio?
findings.claim: Apple's Accessibility HIG page (a general page, not the Materials page) is where a numeric contrast standard actually appears, and it explicitly defers to the third-party WCAG Level AA standard (as implemented in Apple's own Accessibility Inspector tool) rather than defining a proprietary Apple ratio: minimum 4.5:1 for text up to 17pt, 3:1 for 18pt+ or any bold text.
findings.quoted_line: Accessibility Inspector uses the following values from WCAG Level AA as guidance in determining whether your app's colors have an acceptable contrast.
findings.source_title: Accessibility - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What are the exact WCAG AA contrast ratio figures Apple's HIG cites?
findings.claim: The table Apple publishes gives 4.5:1 as the minimum ratio for text up to 17pt (any weight), and 3:1 for 18pt text or any bold text of any size.
findings.quoted_line: Up to 17 pts All 4.5:1 18 pts All 3:1 All Bold 3:1
findings.source_title: Accessibility - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What are the current published default and minimum text sizes per platform?
findings.claim: Current default/minimum text size figures: iOS/iPadOS 17pt default / 11pt minimum; macOS 13pt / 10pt; tvOS 29pt / 23pt; visionOS 17pt / 12pt; watchOS 16pt / 12pt. (These are text-size figures, distinct from the tap-target/control-size figures below.)
findings.quoted_line: iOS, iPadOS 17 pt 11 pt macOS 13 pt 10 pt tvOS 29 pt 23 pt visionOS 17 pt 12 pt watchOS 16 pt 12 pt
findings.source_title: Typography - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What are the current published default and minimum tap target sizes for iOS?
findings.claim: Confirmed as expected: iOS/iPadOS default control (tap target) size is 44x44 pt, minimum is 28x28 pt. The same 44x44/28x28 figures apply to watchOS; macOS uses 28x28pt default/20x20pt minimum (pointer-based); tvOS 66x66pt/56x56pt; visionOS 60x60pt default/28x28pt minimum.
findings.quoted_line: iOS, iPadOS 44x44 pt 28x28 pt
findings.source_title: Accessibility - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Is there corroborating guidance elsewhere in the HIG for the ~44x44pt tap target figure?
findings.claim: The Buttons page independently corroborates the 44x44pt figure as a general-rule hit region for any platform, calling out visionOS's larger 60x60pt figure as the exception.
findings.quoted_line: As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt — in visionOS, 60x60 pt — to ensure that people can select it easily, whether they use a fingertip, a pointer, their eyes, or a remote.
findings.source_title: Buttons - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does macOS support Dynamic Type?
findings.claim: Confirmed: macOS does not support Dynamic Type (the systemwide user text-size-adjustment feature). Dynamic Type is explicitly scoped to iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS elsewhere on the same page.
findings.quoted_line: macOS doesn't support Dynamic Type.
findings.source_title: Typography - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does Apple publish specific durations (in ms) or named easing curves anywhere in the current HIG's Motion page?
findings.claim: No. As expected, the dedicated Motion HIG page contains no millisecond duration values and no named easing-curve terminology (e.g. no 'ease-in-out', no cubic-bezier values, no spring-constant numbers) anywhere in its text. The one place 'easing' is mentioned, it is described only as an automatic, non-configurable system behavior with no name or timing value given.
findings.quoted_line: All layout- and appearance-based animations automatically include built-in easing that plays at the start and end of the animation. You can't turn off or customize easing.
findings.source_title: Motion - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What (if any) numeric values does the Motion page actually contain?
findings.claim: The only two numeric values on the Motion page are: (1) a game frame-rate recommendation of 30-60 fps, which is a rendering-performance target, not an animation duration or curve; and (2) a vestibular-comfort caution against oscillation near 0.2 Hz in visionOS, which is a perceptual-safety threshold, not a UI-animation timing spec. Neither answers the 'duration/easing curve' question in the affirmative.
findings.quoted_line: In most games, maintaining a consistent frame rate of 30 to 60 fps typically results in a smooth, visually appealing experience.
findings.source_title: Motion - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: What is the exact wording of the 0.2 Hz oscillation caution?
findings.claim: Confirmed exact wording of the sole frequency-based numeric caution on the Motion page (visionOS platform-considerations section), included for completeness since it is the only Hz figure on the page.
findings.quoted_line: In particular, you want to avoid showing an oscillation that has a frequency of around 0.2 Hz because people can be very sensitive to this frequency.
findings.source_title: Motion - Apple Developer Documentation (Human Interface Guidelines)

findings.question: Does Apple's HIG function as a design system, a brand book, or both?
findings.claim: The HIG functions as a public engineering-facing design system: every page we read (App icons, Materials, Typography, Layout, Buttons, Motion, Accessibility) is structured around components, platform-by-platform specification tables, and direct cross-references to developer APIs (SwiftUI/UIKit/AppKit/WatchKit types and modifiers). It contains no brand-identity content — no logo/wordmark usage rules, no brand voice or tone guidance, no brand architecture. It is a design system, not a brand book.
findings.source_title: Human Interface Guidelines pages (App icons, Materials, Typography, Layout, Buttons, Motion, Accessibility) - Apple Developer Documentation

findings.question: Does Apple publish a public 'brand book' (identity/mark usage/voice/architecture document) the way it publishes the HIG?
findings.claim: No. What is publicly available under Apple's 'marketing resources' / 'brand' materials is a trademark-permission and legal-usage policy for third parties (developers, resellers, licensees) — governing how they may reference Apple's product names, logo, and badges in their own marketing — not a governance brand book describing Apple's own mark meaning, voice, or brand architecture. The developer.apple.com page titled 'Marketing Resources and Identity Guidelines' is entirely composed of trademark/legal rules (badge specs, product-image rules, naming conventions, trademark symbols, a signed licensing agreement) with no content about brand meaning or voice.
findings.quoted_line: Use only the badge artwork provided in these guidelines. Don't use icons, logos, graphics, or images from www.apple.com to promote your app.
findings.source_title: Marketing Resources and Identity Guidelines - App Store - Apple Developer

findings.question: What is the actual legal document Apple links to for third-party trademark use, and does it read as a brand book?
findings.claim: Apple's own trademark-list page directs users to a document titled 'Guidelines for Using Apple Trademarks' for trademark usage; the linked document (formerly 'Guidelines for Third Parties Using Apple Trademarks and Copyrights') is explicitly scoped to licensees, resellers, developers, and customers wanting to reference Apple's marks — it is a legal/IP-protection policy, not a design/brand governance document.
findings.quoted_line: These guidelines are for Apple licensees, authorized resellers, developers, customers, and other parties wishing to use Apple's trademarks, service marks or images in promotional, advertising, instructional, or reference materials, or on their web sites, products, labels, or packaging.
findings.source_title: Guidelines for Using Apple Trademarks and Copyrights - Apple

findings.question: What is the current total number of standard color roles in Material Design 3, and how are they grouped?
findings.claim: Material's current color-roles page states there are 26 standard color roles in total, organised into six groups: primary, secondary, tertiary, error, surface, and outline.
findings.quoted_line: There are 26 standard color roles organized into six groups: primary, secondary, tertiary, error, surface, and outline
findings.source_title: Color roles – Material Design 3

findings.question: What are the base surface tonal roles currently documented?
findings.claim: The current surface family starts with three base roles: surface, on surface, and on surface variant.
findings.quoted_line: There are three surface roles: Surface: Default color for backgrounds On surface: Text and icons against any surface or surface container color On surface variant: Lower-emphasis color for text and icons against any surface or surface container color
findings.source_title: Color roles – Material Design 3

findings.question: How many surface container tiers exist and what are they?
findings.claim: There are five surface container roles, tiered by emphasis: surface container lowest, low, (default) container, high, and highest.
findings.quoted_line: There are also five surface container roles named based on their level of emphasis: Surface container lowest ... Surface container low ... Surface container ... Surface container high ... Surface container highest
findings.source_title: Color roles – Material Design 3

findings.question: Do surfaceDim and surfaceBright exist as current roles?
findings.claim: Two add-on surface roles exist: surface dim (dimmest in both themes) and surface bright (brightest in both themes).
findings.quoted_line: There are two add-on surface roles: Surface dim: Dimmest surface color in light and dark themes Surface bright: Brightest surface color in light and dark themes
findings.source_title: Color roles – Material Design 3

findings.question: How many tonal surface roles are there in total (surfaceContainerLowest through Highest, surfaceDim, surfaceBright, etc)?
findings.claim: Adding the page's own verified sub-counts (3 base + 5 container tiers + 2 dim/bright add-ons) gives 10 named tonal surface-family roles on the current color-roles page. Two further roles — inverse surface and inverse on surface — exist but are documented separately under 'Inverse colors', not tallied within the page's own surface count. This total of 10 is my arithmetic on the quoted sub-counts above; no single sentence on the page states '10' directly.
findings.source_title: Color roles – Material Design 3

findings.question: Are background, onBackground, and surfaceVariant currently marked DEPRECATED as properties?
findings.claim: In the current (checked today) Jetpack Compose Material3 API reference, the ColorScheme class's background, onBackground and surfaceVariant properties are listed as ordinary public properties with no 'Deprecated' tag on any of them individually.
findings.quoted_line: background — The background color that appears behind scrollable content.
findings.source_title: ColorScheme | API reference | Android Developers

findings.question: If not the properties, what exactly carries the word 'deprecated' on this page?
findings.claim: Only two of the three public ColorScheme() constructor overloads are marked deprecated — the ones that omit the newer 'surfaceContainer' and 'fixed' accent-color parameters — not the color properties themselves, and not via the word 'removed'.
findings.quoted_line: This function is deprecated. Use constructor with additional 'surfaceContainer' roles.
findings.source_title: ColorScheme | API reference | Android Developers

findings.question: Is the material-color-utilities repository currently active/maintained?
findings.claim: The material-color-utilities GitHub repository is active, not archived, with commits from Google's 'Material Eng' team as recently as 10 August 2026 (10 days before this check).
findings.quoted_line: Commits on Aug 10, 2026 — internal change / Internal change / clean up unused GitHub workflow / Refresh README intro and Material links / Fix documentation link
findings.source_title: Commits · material-foundation/material-color-utilities · GitHub

findings.question: Is the Material Theme Builder repository archived, active, or deprecated?
findings.claim: The material-theme-builder GitHub repository (source behind the Material Theme Builder tool) was archived by its owner on 23 July 2026 and is now read-only ('Public archive'), distinct from the still-active material-color-utilities repo.
findings.quoted_line: This repository was archived by the owner on Jul 23, 2026. It is now read-only.
findings.source_title: GitHub - material-foundation/material-theme-builder

findings.topic: Material Theme Builder Figma plugin status
findings.question: Is the Material Theme Builder tool itself still usable even though its repo is archived?
findings.claim: The Figma Community plugin 'Material Theme Builder' (432k users) remains published and installable, but its last version (21) dates to 20 May 2025 — over a year stale — and its own listing recommends migrating away from its legacy 'Surfaces 1–5' feature.
findings.quoted_line: 432k users ... Version 21 on May 20, 2025 ... Surfaces 1–5 will remain in the builder for current users, but we recommend migrating to new surface tokens as soon as possible.
findings.source_title: Material Theme Builder | Figma

findings.question: What are the current named spring categories in M3 Expressive motion?
findings.claim: M3 Expressive's motion physics system defines two spring styles — 'spatial' (position/size/rotation, designed to overshoot and bounce) and 'effects' (color/opacity, designed with no overshoot) — each available at three speeds (fast, default, slow) under two schemes (standard, expressive).
findings.quoted_line: Spatial spring tokens are used for animations that move something on screen... This spring overshoots the final value and bounces into place. ... Effects spring tokens are used to animate properties such as color and opacity animations, where there shouldn't be any overshoot.
findings.source_title: Motion – Material Design 3

findings.question: What damping/stiffness values are published for spatial vs effects springs — are spatial underdamped (overshoot) and effects critically damped?
findings.claim: Google's own AndroidX source (androidx.compose.material3.tokens, generated version v0_14_0) confirms this exactly: expressive spatial springs use damping ratios of 0.8 (default), 0.6 (fast) and 0.8 (slow) — all below 1.0, i.e. underdamped/bouncy — while expressive effects springs use damping ratio 1.0 (critically damped, no overshoot) at every speed; the standard scheme uses 0.9 for all spatial speeds and 1.0 for all effects speeds, with stiffness values ranging 200–3800.
findings.quoted_line: const val SpringDefaultSpatialDamping = 0.8f ... const val SpringDefaultEffectsDamping = 1.0f ... const val SpringFastSpatialDamping = 0.6f
findings.publisher: Google (Android Open Source Project, Android Code Search)
findings.source_title: ExpressiveMotionTokens.kt - Android Code Search

findings.question: What is Android's current published minimum touch target size?
findings.claim: Android's current design guidance states a minimum touch target size of 48dp.
findings.quoted_line: Ensure all touch targets are at least 48 dp, even if this extends past the UI element visual.
findings.source_title: Accessibility | Mobile | Android Developers

findings.question: What is the current adaptive icon canvas size and safe zone diameter?
findings.claim: Adaptive icon layers must be sized to a 108x108dp canvas, with a 66x66dp inner safe zone that is never clipped by an OEM mask, and an 18dp margin reserved on each side for masking/visual effects; the logo itself must be between 48x48dp and 66x66dp.
findings.quoted_line: Size all layers to 108x108 dp. ... Use a logo that's at least 48x48 dp. It must not exceed 66x66 dp, because the inner 66x66 dp of the icon appears within the masked viewport. ... The outer 18 dp on each of the four sides of the layers is reserved for masking and to create visual effects such as parallax or pulsing.
findings.source_title: Adaptive icons | Android Developers

findings.question: Is a themed/monochrome icon layer required for Android 13+?
findings.claim: A monochrome icon layer is not mandatory for the adaptive icon to function, but is required specifically to support Android's per-device icon theming feature introduced in Android 13 (API 33); from Android 16 QPR 2 onward, the OS auto-generates a themed icon for apps that don't supply their own monochrome layer.
findings.quoted_line: starting with Android 13 (API level 33), users can theme their adaptive icons... for apps that have a monochrome layer in their adaptive icon. Starting with Android 16 QPR 2, Android automatically themes app icons for apps that don't provide their own.
findings.source_title: Adaptive icons | Android Developers

findings.topic: Google public brand resources vs governance brand book
findings.question: Does Google publish a public brand book (identity/voice/architecture) separate from Material Design?
findings.claim: Google's public brand page (about.google/brand-resource-center redirects to its Partner Marketing Hub 'Overview') is explicitly framed as a trademark/usage-permission guide for external parties naming or referencing Google — not an internal identity/voice governance brand book. The fuller internal 'Brand Standards' governance site exists but is gated to invited agencies via a Google contact, so its content could not be verified publicly.
findings.quoted_line: If you want to name or refer to Google in your work, these are the guidelines for how to do it, whether you're a business owner, filmmaker, journalist, student, or otherwise. ... If you're part of an agency making work for Google, head to Google's Brand Standards site. If you need access, reach out to your Google contact.
findings.source_title: Overview - Partner Marketing Hub

findings.question: Does Material Design 3 describe itself as a design system or a brand book?
findings.claim: Material Design 3's own homepage describes it explicitly as an engineering/design system, not a brand identity book.
findings.quoted_line: Material Design 3 is Google's open-source design system for building beautiful, usable products.
findings.source_title: Material Design 3 - Google's latest open source design system

findings.topic: DTCG format vs Material's token format
findings.question: Does DTCG appear anywhere in Material's own tooling, or is Material's token format proprietary?
findings.claim: Material's own design-tokens documentation uses a proprietary three-tier dot-separated naming scheme (md.ref / md.sys / md.comp) and does not mention DTCG, the Design Tokens Community Group, or W3C anywhere on the page; the material-color-utilities README likewise contains no such reference. Google is listed generally as a contributing organisation to the separate, unrelated W3C DTCG specification, but Material's own tooling does not adopt or reference that format.
findings.quoted_line: All token names in a design system start with the system name (such as "md" for Material Design) ... Organizations represented include Adobe, Amazon, Google, Baidu, Sony, Microsoft, Meta, Sketch, Salesforce, Shopify, Figma, Framer, Cisco, Intuit, New York Times, GM, Disney, Anima, Pinterest, Tokens Studio, Penpot, Knapsack, Supernova, zeroheight, and many others.
findings.publisher: Google (Material Design); W3C Design Tokens Community Group
findings.source_title: Design tokens – Material Design 3

findings.claim: Instagram's official Apple App Store listing, read live today, carries an explicit sub-brand endorsement line directly under its tagline, confirming Meta uses a named 'from Meta' convention for Instagram in metadata Meta itself controls.
findings.quoted_line: Share yours on Instagram. — From Meta
findings.source_title: Instagram App - App Store
findings.publisher: Apple App Store (listing content authored/submitted by Instagram, Inc. / Meta)

findings.question: Is the 'from Meta' endorsement consistent across app-store platforms, not just Apple's?
findings.claim: The identical endorsement tagline appears verbatim on Instagram's Google Play listing, read live today, showing the convention is applied consistently by Meta across both major app stores rather than being an Apple-specific quirk.
findings.quoted_line: Share yours on Instagram. —From Meta
findings.source_title: Instagram - Apps on Google Play
findings.publisher: Google Play Store (listing content authored/submitted by Instagram, Inc. / Meta)

findings.question: Does WhatsApp's own listing use the same endorsement, and does it disclose a user count?
findings.claim: WhatsApp's own App Store description opens by naming itself 'WhatsApp from Meta' in the first sentence of body copy (not just a subtitle), and states a specific global user count in the same sentence.

findings.publisher: Apple App Store (listing content authored/submitted by WhatsApp Inc. / Meta)

findings.question: Does the 'from Meta' convention extend beyond app-store metadata into Instagram's own website?
findings.claim: Instagram's own official website (about.instagram.com), read live today, labels a footer navigation link 'Instagram from Meta', showing the endorsement convention is used on Instagram's owned-and-operated web presence, not only in app-store copy.

findings.question: Does Facebook's own listing carry the same 'from Meta' endorsement as Instagram and WhatsApp?
findings.claim: Facebook's own App Store listing, read live today, carries no 'from Meta' tagline anywhere in its title, subtitle or description; its Developer field is instead listed directly as 'Meta Platforms, Inc.' — suggesting the endorsement device is used for acquired sibling products rather than for the company's eponymous flagship app.

findings.question: How is Threads positioned relative to Meta and to Instagram?
findings.claim: Threads is presented on the App Store as 'Threads, an Instagram app' with Developer listed as 'Instagram, Inc.' (not 'Meta Platforms, Inc.' and not a 'from Meta' tag), consistent with Meta's own company-info history page describing Threads as built by a product team rather than launched as a direct sibling brand — a second tier of endorsement, product-of-a-product rather than product-of-Meta.
findings.quoted_line: Threads, a new text-sharing app built by the Instagram team, launches.
findings.source_title: Threads App - App Store / Company info | Meta
findings.publisher: Apple App Store; About Meta (company-info page)

findings.question: Is there one unified visual system across Meta's products, or does each keep separate identity governance?
findings.claim: Meta operates a single 'Brand Resource Center' microsite that is explicitly organised product-by-product — Meta, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads each have their own separate named guidelines page for logo, colour and usage — read live today, confirming a 'house of brands' architecture (separately governed sub-brands) rather than one umbrella visual identity stamped across all products.
findings.source_title: Meta brand resources and guidelines | Brand Resource Center

findings.question: Does Meta require its products to co-brand with each other or with Meta in third-party usage?
findings.claim: Instagram's own product-specific brand guidelines (part of the same Brand Resource Center, read live today) instruct third parties not to imply partnership/endorsement, to keep the Instagram name undiluted, and to avoid mentioning Instagram alongside Facebook in the same advertising spot except for generic 'Follow us on...' calls to action — evidence each product is governed as a distinct sibling brand rather than a required joint presentation.
findings.source_title: Instagram brand assets and guidelines | Brand Resource Center

findings.question: Is Meta's own published guidance for its corporate mark a design system or a brand book?
findings.claim: What Meta publishes for its own corporate logo, read live today, is a brand book — colour variants, minimum size, clear space, a gated internal 'Brand Review' approval process, and trademark legal terms — with no components, design tokens or code of any kind, i.e. the opposite of an engineering design system.
findings.quoted_line: never be used below 12px/5mm
findings.source_title: Meta brand resources and guidelines | Brand Resource Center

findings.question: Does Meta publish any public design system at all, comparable in kind (not brand) to Material or HIG?
findings.claim: Contrary to the assumption that Meta publishes nothing comparable, Meta does now publish a genuine public, open-source design system called Astryx (astryx.atmeta.com), which went into Beta on 18 June 2026 and, read live today, documents 150-170+ accessible React components, design tokens, themes, templates and a CLI — a real engineering-contract design system in the technical sense.
findings.quoted_line: matured within Meta for the last eight years and powers over 13,000 apps
findings.source_title: Introducing Astryx by Meta: an open source design system built for how we build now

findings.question: Does Astryx function as an expression of Meta's own product brand identity, the way HIG/Material express Apple's/Google's?
findings.claim: Astryx's own launch post, read live today, explicitly frames itself as brand-neutral, white-label tooling and frames the alternative — adopting a 'big company' system — as the problem it was built to avoid; this means Astryx is not analogous to Apple's HIG or Google's Material as a public codification of the parent's own visible product identity, it is a generic engineering toolkit Meta happens to have open-sourced.
