findings.topic: IBM Carbon Design System — DTCG token format
findings.question: Does Carbon publish design tokens in W3C DTCG format?
findings.claim: Carbon's own GitHub repository contains live, DTCG-formatted token source files today — e.g. packages/themes/src/dtcg/white.json and packages/motion/src/dtcg/motion.json — using the official DTCG schema, $type, $value and $description fields, with alias-style value references (e.g. a token's $value pointing to "{gray.80}"). This confirms an actual, working DTCG implementation, not just a proposal.
findings.quoted_line: "$schema": "https://tr.designtokens.org/format/" ... "background-inverse": { "$type": "color", "$value": "{gray.80}" }

findings.topic: IBM Carbon Design System — DTCG migration status
findings.question: What does Carbon's own tracking issue say about DTCG adoption?
findings.claim: Carbon's GitHub issue #22437, "Implement Design Token Spec DTCG," directed the team to refactor the token source and build pipeline to follow the DTCG spec using the .tokens.json format. It closed on 17 July 2026, and linked pull requests (#22743 motion tokens, #22870 Style Dictionary v5 migration) merged in late July/early August 2026, indicating the migration is substantially complete for the motion and themes/color packages as of today.
findings.quoted_line: refactor the source(s) of truth and build process to follow the spec created by the Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG)

findings.topic: IBM Carbon Design System — brand vs. design system
findings.question: How does Carbon separate IBM's brand identity from the public design system?
findings.claim: Carbon's own docs state it does NOT treat brand and design system as separate governed layers: Carbon is positioned as the very expression of the IBM brand, and brand compliance is achieved through Carbon compliance, not through a distinct brand rulebook sitting above it.
findings.quoted_line: Carbon compliance by the IBM community is critically important to the IBM brand. Carbon is the digital expression of the IBM brand and the chassis upon which all products and digital experiences are built.

findings.topic: IBM Carbon Design System — token layering model (color)
findings.question: What is Carbon's token layering model, in Carbon's own layer names?
findings.claim: For color specifically, Carbon's live docs name three layers: "Core Tokens" (global colors used across all components), "Component Tokens" (colors scoped to one component only and never reused elsewhere), and "AI Tokens" (a separate suite reserved for AI-styled UI). This is Carbon's actual current terminology, not the generic "global/alias/component" naming some third-party write-ups attribute to it.
findings.quoted_line: Core tokens are global colors that are used across components... Some components have their own specific color tokens, known as component tokens... and should never be used for anything other than their own component.

findings.topic: IBM Carbon Design System — general token model and categories
findings.question: What is Carbon's token model across all token types (not just color)?
findings.claim: Across all token types, Carbon defines a Token/Role/Value model — a token is a role-based identifier, a role is the token's fixed usage, and a value is the actual style assigned per theme — and groups all tokens into four categories: Color, Spacing, Typography, and Global (the last covering cross-cutting things like layer usage or border width).
findings.quoted_line: Token: A role-based identifier that assigns a value to a theme. Tokens are universal and never change across themes | Role: The systematic usage(s) of a token. Roles cannot be changed between themes

findings.topic: Correction: Carbon's actual vs. commonly-assumed token terminology
findings.question: Does Carbon itself use the words "global tokens / alias tokens / component tokens" as some summaries claim?
findings.claim: I searched Carbon's live docs, its @carbon/themes README, and its DTCG JSON source files directly: the word "alias" does not appear anywhere in them. The classic "global → alias → component" framing found in web summaries and a 2023-era GitHub discussion describes proposed community models, not Carbon's own shipped terminology, which is Core/Component/AI Tokens (color) and Color/Spacing/Typography/Global categories (general).

findings.question: Does Spectrum tie a colour's use to which background layer it sits on?
findings.claim: Spectrum formally defines exactly three named background layers for application framing — background base, background layer 1, and background layer 2 — each mapped to a specific gray token per theme, and explicitly states these layer colours are themselves "alias tokens" within Spectrum's design-token system.
findings.quoted_line: Spectrum provides three background layer color options for use in application framing: background layer 1, background layer 2, and background base.

findings.topic: Adobe Spectrum — contrast generation relative to background
findings.question: How does Spectrum generate colour contrast relative to a background?
findings.claim: Spectrum's colour system computes gray and colour token values by targeting specific contrast ratios against a chosen background colour value; Spectrum's own glossary defines a "color theme" as the full set of tokens and values relative to one specific background colour, which is the formal contrast-pair mechanism behind the system.
findings.quoted_line: Color theme: The full set of color tokens and their color values relative to a specific background color.

findings.question: Does Spectrum define fixed colour pairs keyed to specific background indices?
findings.claim: Spectrum has an explicit "two-tone color pairing" rule: a low-index shade (index 100, e.g. magenta-100) is fixed as the background, paired with a specific high-index shade (index 900 in light theme, e.g. magenta-900) as the icon/illustration colour placed on it — a literal, named colour-to-background pairing model.
findings.quoted_line: To create two-tone color pairs, use the 100 index of your color for the background (e.g., magenta-100). The icon or illustration should use the 900 index in light theme (e.g., magenta-900).

findings.topic: Adobe Spectrum — Windows High Contrast Mode guidance
findings.question: Does Spectrum publish guidance on Windows High Contrast Mode?
findings.claim: Spectrum's "Inclusive design" page has a dedicated checkpoint titled "High contrast mode in Windows," stating WHCM must be supported by all Adobe web-based and Windows applications, and that Spectrum component documentation will show visual references for the default Windows high-contrast black theme. This is guidance/description, not a full alternate visual theme shipped on the docs site itself.
findings.quoted_line: Windows high contrast mode is a setting that replaces all colors in the operating system to a simplified high contrast color palette... and should be supported by all Adobe web-based and Windows applications.

findings.topic: Adobe Spectrum — Windows High Contrast Mode implementation
findings.question: Is WHCM support actually implemented in Spectrum's code, not just described?
findings.claim: Adobe's spectrum-css component library implements Windows High Contrast Mode today via the modern CSS Forced Colors Mode media query in live component stylesheets, mapping component colours to CSS system-colour keywords (e.g. CanvasText, ButtonText, Highlight) inside a block explicitly commented "windows high contrast mode."
findings.quoted_line: /* windows high contrast mode */ @media (forced-colors: active) { .spectrum-Radio { --highcontrast-radio-neutral-content-color: CanvasText;

findings.topic: Adobe Spectrum — brand vs. design system separation
findings.question: Does Spectrum separate Adobe's brand identity from the design system publicly?
findings.claim: Adobe's own design blog states the opposite of a separation: the organisation that runs Spectrum is explicitly described as also responsible for Adobe's overall brand, and Spectrum 2's colour system was deliberately rebuilt to use Adobe's brand colours specifically to integrate brand into product experience — brand is one design workstream feeding Spectrum, not a separately governed document.
findings.quoted_line: Shawn runs Spectrum—an organization collectively responsible for the overall brand and experience of Adobe's products.

findings.question: What colour roles does Primer define that are specifically about surviving light/dark theme switching?
findings.claim: Primer organises colour into three tiers: Base tokens (raw values, e.g. color-scale-pink-5) which do NOT respect colour mode and must never be used directly; Functional tokens (e.g. fgColor-*, bgColor-*, borderColor-*) which DO respect colour mode and are the tier meant to survive theme switching; and Component/pattern tokens for narrower one-off cases. The naming convention prefixes the CSS property affected (fgColor = text/icon colour, bgColor = background, borderColor = border) and suffixes a semantic role (default, muted, accent, danger, success, onEmphasis, etc.) rather than a hue name.
findings.quoted_line: Base color tokens are the lowest level tokens and map directly to a raw value. They are only to be used as a reference for functional and component/pattern tokens. Base color tokens don't respect color modes and should never be used directly in code or design.

findings.topic: GitHub Primer — how a functional token switches value per theme
findings.question: Confirmation that a single functional token name resolves to different hex values in light vs dark mode.
findings.claim: Primer states explicitly that a functional token like bgColor-default automatically changes its resolved value depending on which colour mode (theme) is active — the token name is stable, only the value shifts.
findings.quoted_line: As an example of how color tokens work, when bgColor-default is referenced for a background color, the value of that token will automatically change depending on the color mode.

findings.question: Any naming/structural convention worth flagging for a developer-facing brand.
findings.claim: Primer's light and dark neutral scales are numbered in opposite directions (light scale starts at white, dark scale starts at black) specifically so that light and dark themes can share the same functional token names without needing custom per-theme overrides — a structural trick, not just a naming one.
findings.quoted_line: The light and dark scale directions are inverted, with the light scale starting with white and the dark scale starting with black. By inverting the scales, light and dark themes are able to share many of the same functional color tokens without custom overrides.

findings.question: What roles/naming convention exists worth noting for a developer audience.
findings.claim: Primer defines 8 named semantic colour roles, each tied to one stated meaning rather than a hue: accent (links, selected/active/focus, neutral info), success (primary buttons, positive states), attention (warnings, in-progress), danger (danger buttons, errors), open, closed, done (task/PR/workflow states), and sponsors (GitHub Sponsors branding). Each role additionally carries -muted and -emphasis background/border variants and an -onEmphasis foreground variant for text placed on an emphasis background.
findings.quoted_line: Semantic colors are typically used to communicate status, action, or emphasis. Each semantic color is tied to a role with a specific meaning.

findings.question: How many themes does the light/dark system actually span?
findings.claim: Primer's colour system is not simply binary light/dark — it is built to support nine distinct themes (including colour-blind and high-contrast variants) sharing the same functional token names.
findings.quoted_line: GitHub's UI offers two color modes, light and dark. Primer supports both color modes across nine themes. Every pattern in Primer is built to work across all color modes out of the box.

findings.topic: GitHub Primer — actual variable names (primary reference page)
findings.question: Direct confirmation of the naming convention as shipped in CSS.
findings.claim: The live Primer colour reference page lists the functional variables exactly as documented — e.g. --fgColor-accent, --fgColor-danger, --fgColor-onEmphasis, --bgColor-accent-emphasis, --bgColor-accent-muted, --borderColor-danger-emphasis — and states the page only shows one theme's resolved values at a time, confirming the same names carry different values in Storybook's other themes.
findings.quoted_line: This page only shows colors in the site's active theme ("light" or "dark"). Use the Primitives Storybook to see colors in all themes.

findings.topic: GitHub Primer — design system vs brand book
findings.question: Which does Primer publish?
findings.claim: Primer self-identifies on its homepage as GitHub's design system (tokens, components, accessibility guidance, Storybook code) — this is a public engineering contract. GitHub separately maintains a distinct 'Brand toolkit' and 'Primer Brand UI' for marketing/identity work, so the identity-governance layer (brand book) is a separate, smaller offering alongside the much larger engineering design system.
findings.quoted_line: Primer / The design system for GitHub

findings.topic: Atlassian — voice and tone, principle layer
findings.question: Is Atlassian's voice/tone guidance just abstract principles?
findings.claim: At the top level, Atlassian's voice is defined as three personality traits (Bold, Optimistic, Practical with a wink) expressed through six situational tone principles (Inform to build trust, Empower to inspire action, Encourage people along the path, Motivate by showing possibilities, Satisfy by meeting expectations, Delight with unexpectedly pleasing experiences), each mapped to the user's emotional state and to specific UI surfaces (flags, error messages, modals, spotlights) where it should or shouldn't be applied.
findings.quoted_line: Our voice is essentially Atlassian's personality and is made up of the following traits: Bold, Optimistic, Practical, with a wink

findings.topic: Atlassian — operational content rules beyond principles
findings.question: Does Atlassian give concrete, GOV.UK-style rules (banned words, sentence patterns) underneath the voice principles?
findings.claim: Yes — underneath the principle layer, Atlassian's Style, grammar and punctuation page gives dozens of concrete, testable Do/Don't rules: mandatory sentence case (not Title Case) in headings/buttons, mandatory active voice, present tense preferred, no periods in headings, an Oxford comma requirement, exact keyboard shortcuts for curly quotes/em dashes, and banned constructions such as 'e.g.', 'i.e.', 'etc.' and '&'. This is the same operational register as GOV.UK's style guide, not just principles.
findings.quoted_line: Don't use 'e.g.', 'i.e.', 'etc.', or '&' as they're not localization friendly and can be confusing for users of assistive technologies.

findings.question: Concrete sentence-pattern rule example.
findings.claim: Atlassian mandates active voice as a hard rule tied explicitly back to brand voice, with a worked Do/Don't pair, not left as a vague preference.
findings.quoted_line: Use active voice whenever possible as it improves readability and reflects Atlassian's voice and tone.

findings.question: Example of a numeric operational rule.
findings.claim: Atlassian caps list length as an explicit numeric rule rather than a vague guideline.
findings.quoted_line: Try to limit lists to 6 items or less. If there are more items, make multiple lists.

findings.question: Is there a fuller banned/approved word list?
findings.claim: Atlassian references an internal vocabulary/glossary list ('go/vocab') for specific word choices, but this is explicitly gated to Atlassian staff and not published on the public site, so its contents could not be verified today.
findings.quoted_line: For specific vocabulary and to view our internal word list and glossary, head to go/vocab (Atlassians only).

findings.topic: Atlassian — design system vs brand book
findings.question: Which does Atlassian publish?
findings.claim: atlassian.design self-labels its main offering 'Design system' (Foundations, Components, Patterns, Tools, plus the Atlaskit component library) — an engineering contract that also folds in content-design/voice-and-tone guidance. A separate 'Brand kit' is listed independently in the site footer alongside the design system, indicating Atlassian treats brand identity governance as a distinct, smaller artifact from the design system proper.
findings.quoted_line: Other libraries Atlaskit​ Forge UI Kit​ Brand kit​

findings.question: Does each of the 12 steps have a stated job?
findings.claim: Yes — Radix Colors publishes an explicit use-case table assigning one primary job to each of the 12 steps: 1 App background, 2 Subtle background, 3 UI element background, 4 Hovered UI element background, 5 Active/Selected UI element background, 6 Subtle borders and separators, 7 UI element border and focus rings, 8 Hovered UI element border, 9 Solid backgrounds, 10 Hovered solid backgrounds, 11 Low-contrast text, 12 High-contrast text.
findings.quoted_line: There are 12 steps in each scale. Each step was designed for at least one specific use case.

findings.question: Detail on steps 3-5 job split.
findings.claim: Steps 3, 4 and 5 are explicitly assigned to a component's normal, hover, and pressed/selected background states respectively.
findings.quoted_line: Step 3 is for normal states. Step 4 is for hover states. Step 5 is for pressed or selected states.

findings.topic: Radix Colors — contrast guarantee for text steps
findings.question: Is there a stated, testable contrast guarantee behind steps 11/12?
findings.claim: Radix states that its text steps (11 and 12) are engineered to a specific measured contrast guarantee against a step-2 background from the same scale, using the APCA contrast metric — not just a subjective 'low/high contrast' label.
findings.quoted_line: Steps 11 and 12—which are designed for text—are guaranteed to Lc 60 and Lc 90 APCA contrast ratio on top of a step 2 background from the same scale.

findings.question: Who publishes/maintains Radix Colors today?
findings.claim: The current live Radix Colors site attributes the project to WorkOS ('Made by WorkOS'), confirming WorkOS is the present-day publisher/maintainer as of this research date.
findings.quoted_line: Radix Homepage Made by WorkOS

findings.topic: Radix Colors — design system vs brand book vs primitive
findings.question: Which category does Radix Colors fall into?
findings.claim: Radix Colors is neither a full design system nor a brand book — it is a primitive colour-token library (palettes plus a use-case/aliasing methodology) meant to be consumed inside someone else's design system or brand implementation. No components, voice/tone, or identity-governance content is published alongside it.

findings.question: What does USWDS's naming actually encode (family vs lightness)?
findings.claim: USWDS colour token names encode a hue family plus a lightness step (e.g. red-50, green-cool-10, indigo-warm-60v) — the name itself communicates hue family and how light/dark the swatch is, but does NOT literally spell out a pass/fail accessibility verdict.
findings.quoted_line: Color is any specific swatch in our system color token palette, like red-50, green-cool-10, or indigo-warm-60v.

findings.question: How is lightness standardised across colour families?
findings.claim: USWDS uses a standardised 100-point 'grade' scale (0 = pure white, 100 = pure black) applied consistently across all 24 colour families, so a given grade number means the same lightness regardless of hue family — this is the mechanism, not a literal AA/AAA label in the name.
findings.quoted_line: USWDS uses a 100-point scale to communicate a color token's grade, where 0 is pure white and 100 is pure black.

findings.topic: USWDS — 'magic number' contrast heuristic (answers Q4 directly)
findings.question: Does USWDS encode contrast information into the token/colour name itself?
findings.claim: No — the token name does not itself state whether a colour passes WCAG AA. Instead, USWDS provides a separate calculation rule called the 'magic number' (the arithmetic difference between two colours' grade numbers) that a designer applies manually to two chosen tokens to predict their contrast tier. So accessibility is derivable from the naming system via a rule of thumb, but is not baked directly into any single token's name.
findings.quoted_line: We call the difference in grade between any two colors the magic number. Magic numbers have the following contrast implications: A magic number of 40+ results in WCAG 2.0 AA Large Text contrast (example: gray-90 and indigo-warm-50v). A magic number of 50+ results in WCAG 2.0 AA contrast or AAA Large Text contrast (example: gray-90 and red-40). A magic number of 70+ results in WCAG 2.0 AAA contrast (example: gray-10 and red-80).

findings.question: How many grade steps exist per colour family and what's the range?
findings.claim: Each USWDS colour family is built from 10 named grade steps spanning 5 to 90 (with 0 and 100 reserved for pure white/black), each grade regularised to a fixed luminance band so contrast math is predictable across the whole 24-family system.
findings.quoted_line: Each color family has 10 grades, which fall between 5 and 90. Pure white is the equivalent of grade 0, and pure black is the equivalent of grade 100.

findings.topic: USWDS — legal contrast baseline it targets
findings.question: What contrast ratio does USWDS's system target as its floor?
findings.claim: USWDS ties its whole grade/magic-number system back to a specific legal contrast floor: Section 508 (which it says aligns with WCAG 2.0 Level AA) requiring 4.5:1 contrast for most text and 3:1 for large text.
findings.quoted_line: The baseline AA contrast standard is 4.5:1 for most text and 3:1 for large text (19px+ bold or 24px+ normal text).

findings.topic: USWDS — scale of the system palette
findings.question: How many colour families exist in the full System token set?
findings.claim: The complete USWDS System palette spans 24 colour families, of which any individual project is expected to adopt only a small role-based subset for its own identity.
findings.quoted_line: This subset of tokens will use only a few color families from the 24 color families available in the set of System tokens.

findings.question: Which category does USWDS fall into?
findings.claim: USWDS is explicitly a design system (design tokens plus components/patterns for building federal government sites), organised around theme/state/system token layers rather than around a single brand's identity governance — individual agencies are expected to layer their own project-level identity on top of the shared System tokens.
findings.quoted_line: USWDS organizes its color tokens into theme tokens, state tokens, and System tokens. System tokens are the complete set of colors available from USWDS.

findings.question: Does Mozilla publish a public brand book AND a separate public design system?
findings.claim: Yes. Mozilla's own design-system homepage explicitly names and separates the two: Acorn is the public design system for the Firefox product (tokens, components, content, platform guidelines), while a distinct resource called 'Firefox Brand Guidelines' covers positioning, voice and tone, and visual elements (i.e. a brand book), and a third resource, Mozilla Protocol, is a separate design system for marketing websites.
findings.quoted_line: Firefox Brand Guidelines — These guidelines document the Brand System as it applies to brand design and marketing applications. It includes positioning, voice and tone, and visual elements. Mozilla Protocol — Mozilla maintains a design system used for marketing websites.
findings.source_title: Acorn – Acorn Design System (homepage)

findings.question: What does Acorn (the design system) actually contain?
findings.claim: Acorn documents Firefox's current design across desktop, iOS and Android, organised into Get Started, Foundations, Content, Desktop, Mobile and Support sections — i.e. an engineering-facing design system, not identity governance.
findings.quoted_line: Acorn is the design system for the Firefox desktop, as well as our iOS and Android browsers. It’s a curated library of design, content, and development decisions that built the Firefox you know and love.
findings.source_title: Acorn – Acorn Design System (homepage)

findings.question: How does Mozilla itself label its various design resources (design system vs brand/style guide, public vs private)?
findings.claim: Mozilla's own internal glossary page explicitly labels Acorn and Protocol as public-facing design systems, Nebula as a private design system, and 'Mozilla.design' (which now redirects to the brand.mozilla.com brand portal) as the brand guidelines/style guide for Firefox and Mozilla.
findings.quoted_line: Acorn is public-facing. [...] Protocol is public-facing. [...] Nebula [design system]: A private design system for Privacy and Security products. [...] Mozilla.design [style guide]: Brand guidelines for Firefox and Mozilla.
findings.source_title: Mozilla design systems landscape – Acorn Design System

findings.question: What does Mozilla's public brand book (brand.mozilla.com) actually contain, section by section?
findings.claim: The live Firefox Brand portal on brand.mozilla.com is a genuine, comprehensive brand book with a public 'GUIDELINES' navigation group (Overview, Voice & Tone, Visual Elements, Product Design) and a 'DOWNLOADS' group of asset libraries (Logo, Mascot, Motion, Environment, Pictogram, Type, Audio). The Visual Elements document itself breaks down into Color, Logos, Mascot, Environment, Pictograms, Typography, Motion, and Brand in Action pages, and every page checked is set to public visibility (no login). Note on method: the human-rendered page threw a client-side error in this automated browser (a JS bug in the Frontify-vendors bundle used to host the portal), so this structure was confirmed by reading the portal's own public API responses directly rather than the rendered page — the underlying data is Mozilla's own, fetched live today.
findings.source_title: Mozilla Brand Portal – Firefox Brand navigation data (public API)

findings.question: Does Wikimedia publish both a brand book and a design system?
findings.claim: Yes. Codex (doc.wikimedia.org/codex) is Wikimedia's public design system (tokens, Vue/CSS components, icons). Separately, the Wikimedia Foundation Governance Wiki publishes a detailed public visual identity guide covering the Wikipedia puzzle globe, wordmark, construction rules and permitted variants — a genuine brand/mark book, distinct from Codex.
findings.quoted_line: The distinctive Wikipedia identity has evolved over the years since it was introduced in 2003 [...] The hero version of the puzzle globe shows characters from 18 language sets: Armenian, Khmer, Japanese (Katakana), Geez, Guarani, Greek, Latin, Arabic, Devanagari, Traditional Chinese, Cyrillic, Korean, Georgian, Kannada, Hebrew, Thai, Tibetan, Tamil.
findings.source_title: Legal:Visual identity guidelines – Wikimedia Foundation Governance Wiki

findings.question: How does Codex handle non-Latin scripts, RTL and CJK?
findings.claim: Codex treats bidirectionality (LTR/RTL) as a first-class, dedicated concern with its own detailed style-guide page and explicit mirroring rules for icons, buttons, text alignment, dates, addresses and more. The page explicitly classifies scripts: Latin, Cyrillic, Armenian, Georgian and Devanagari (an Indic script) as LTR; notes Chinese and Japanese follow LTR in digital contexts despite RTL/vertical print traditions; and classifies Arabic and Hebrew as RTL.
findings.quoted_line: Languages with left-to-right directionality (LTR) are those with Latin script (English, Spanish, French, German, etc.), Cyrillic (as Russian and Bulgarian), Armenian, Georgian, and Devanagari. Chinese and Japanese also follow the LTR system in digital experiences, although they traditionally use top-to-bottom and RTL directions in printing and writing. [...] Conversely, languages with right-to-left directionality (RTL), such as Arabic or Hebrew, are read from right to left.
findings.source_title: Bidirectionality | Codex
findings.publisher: Wikimedia Foundation / Codex Design System Team

findings.question: Does Codex build internationalisation/directionality into its components and icons as a first-class feature?
findings.claim: Codex's own README lists internationalisation and translatability as headline product features, not an afterthought, and states the icon set includes language and directionality variants.
findings.quoted_line: Components: for building usable, accessible, translatable applications. Codex contains Vue 3 components and CSS-only components [...] Icons: a collection of icons with language and directionality variants [...] Codex features: Wide-ranging support for internationalization and global usage
findings.source_title: design/codex README.md – Gitiles (Wikimedia Gerrit)

findings.question: Under what licence is Codex actually released?
findings.claim: Codex's own source code is licensed GPL-2.0 (or later), not MIT. This corrects the generic 'code under MIT' line in the design.wikimedia.org site footer, which is shared boilerplate across Wikimedia sites and does not describe Codex's own repository licence; the npm registry page and the repository's own LICENSE file both confirm GPL.
findings.quoted_line: GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 2, June 1991
findings.source_title: LICENSE file, design/codex repository (Gitiles); corroborated by npm package page (License: GPL-2.0+)

findings.question: Is Ant Design's documentation genuinely bilingual, and how is it structured?
findings.claim: Ant Design's documentation is structured as separate parallel Markdown files per component, one per locale (e.g. index.en-US.md and index.zh-CN.md sitting side by side in the same directory), not a single source auto-translated at build time. A header language-toggle switches the whole site, and the URL for a translated page gets a distinct '-cn' suffix (e.g. /components/button vs /components/button-cn).
findings.source_title: ant-design/components/button directory listing – GitHub
findings.publisher: Ant Design / Ant Group open-source community

findings.question: Is the Chinese content independently authored rather than a translation of the English?
findings.claim: The live Chinese Button page includes a Chinese-specific typographic guidance item with no English-language equivalent on the English Button page, indicating the Chinese docs are written to address Chinese-specific concerns rather than being a mechanical translation of the English source.
findings.quoted_line: 移除两个汉字之间的空格 (translation: 'remove the space between two Chinese characters') — present as a listed demo/topic on the Chinese Button page, with no corresponding item on the English Button page.
findings.source_title: 按钮 Button - Ant Design (Chinese locale)

findings.question: Does Ant Design/Ant Group publish a separate public brand book alongside the design system?
findings.claim: No separate public brand book (logo usage, voice/tone, brand architecture) was found for Ant Design distinct from the design system itself. Ant Design's own 'spec' section (Design Values, Global Styles, Colors, Design Patterns, Principles) is part of the design system's design-language documentation, not a standalone brand governance document.
findings.source_title: Introduction – Ant Design docs/spec

findings.question: Does GOV.UK publish both a public brand book and a public design system, and are they actually separate resources?
findings.claim: Yes, and they are hosted as clearly separate public sites. design-system.service.gov.uk is the design system (styles, components, patterns, code, MIT-licensed). brand.design-system.service.gov.uk is titled 'GOV.UK Brand Guidelines' and is a distinct brand book covering the graphic device (the dot), the logo system (wordmark + crown), colour, typography, data/chart branding, and 'brand in use', with assets downloadable from a separate GitHub repo.
findings.quoted_line: How to use the GOV.UK brand. Help users find, understand and trust the GOV.UK brand. [...] Logo system: How the GOV.UK wordmark and crown work together in different contexts. [...] Get brand assets: You can find and download brand element and asset files in the govuk-brand-assets repository on GitHub.
findings.source_title: GOV.UK Brand Guidelines (homepage)

findings.question: What licence is the GOV.UK Design System's code released under?
findings.claim: The GOV.UK Design System's code is public and released under the MIT licence.
findings.quoted_line: The GOV.UK Design System’s code is public and freely available under a Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) license. You can find our code repositories on GitHub, where we code in the open.
findings.source_title: Components – GOV.UK Design System

findings.question: Does GOV.UK state an explicit target reading age (e.g. 'age 9') on its current, primary content-design guidance?
findings.claim: The current (checked today) official GOV.UK content and publishing guidance page on plain language does NOT state a numeric target reading age. Instead it mandates plain English generally and gives concrete, quantified structural rules: paragraphs of no more than 5 sentences, and splitting sentences longer than 25 words. The widely-repeated 'reading age of 9' figure was not found on this current primary page — it appears mainly on secondary/derivative sources (see could_not_verify).
findings.quoted_line: Plain English is mandatory for all of GOV.UK. [...] Paragraphs should have no more than 5 sentences each. Try to split up sentences that are over 25 words long.
findings.source_title: Use clear language – GOV.UK content and publishing guidance

findings.question: Does the GOV.UK Design System state, as policy, that components are backed by disclosed research evidence?
findings.claim: Yes. The Design System's own 'Get started' page states as explicit policy that every published style, component or pattern includes disclosure of how and when it was tested in user research.
findings.quoted_line: When we publish new styles, components or patterns we include details of how and when it’s been tested in user research. This should help you decide whether it’s something you can use or adapt for your service.
findings.source_title: Get started – GOV.UK Design System

findings.question: What does a GOV.UK component's disclosed research evidence actually look like in practice?
findings.claim: Each component page carries a standard 'Research on this component' section giving who tested it, when, and with how many/what kind of users, followed by 'Known issues and gaps' and 'Services using this component' (naming real live government services) and 'Next steps' (open research questions). For the Character count component this discloses a 2017 GDS usability study and a 2022 accessibility fix.
findings.quoted_line: In 2017, the Government Digital Service (GDS) developed and tested this component in a prototype of the ‘Apply for a temporary event notice’ service. During this research, the component was tested with 17 users, including those with low digital skills and users with disabilities. In 2022, the GOV.UK Design System team updated the component to make it more accessible, stopping the character count being announced twice by some screenreaders.
findings.source_title: Character count – GOV.UK Design System

findings.question: Is the 'Research on this component' format consistent across different components (second example)?
findings.claim: The Accordion component page follows the same evidence format: a dated note on what was fixed and why, a link to a fuller research write-up, and an explicit 'Known issues and gaps' list of open questions the team wants more user research on.
findings.quoted_line: We updated this component in December 2021 to solve an accessibility issue where the buttons and section labels might be mistaken for links. Read about the research and development that went into improving the accordion component.
findings.source_title: Accordion – GOV.UK Design System

findings.question: Is WCAG 2.2 a W3C Recommendation, and what is the exact publication date?
findings.claim: WCAG 2.2 is a W3C Recommendation, published 12 December 2024.
findings.quoted_line: W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024
findings.source_title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2

findings.question: What contrast ratio does SC 1.4.3 require for normal text?
findings.claim: SC 1.4.3 (Level AA) requires text and images of text to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, with large-scale text as the stated exception.
findings.quoted_line: The visual presentation of text and images of text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for the following: Large Text
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 — Success Criterion 1.4.3

findings.question: What contrast ratio does SC 1.4.3 require for large-scale text?
findings.claim: Large-scale text (and images of large-scale text) need only a 3:1 contrast ratio under SC 1.4.3.
findings.quoted_line: Large-scale text and images of large-scale text have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 — Success Criterion 1.4.3

findings.question: What is the exact point-size threshold that defines 'large text' for SC 1.4.3?
findings.claim: WCAG 2.2's glossary defines large-scale text as at least 18 point, or 14 point bold, type (or the CJK equivalent size) — not simply '18pt or 14pt' without the bold qualifier on the smaller size.
findings.quoted_line: large scale (text) with at least 18 point or 14 point bold or font size that would yield equivalent size for Chinese, Japanese and Korean (CJK) fonts
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 — Glossary, definition of 'large scale (text)'

findings.question: What contrast ratio does SC 1.4.11 require for UI components and graphical objects?
findings.claim: SC 1.4.11 (Level AA) requires a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colours for user interface components and graphical objects.
findings.quoted_line: The visual presentation of the following have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s): User Interface Components
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 — Success Criterion 1.4.11

findings.topic: Absence of an AAA-level non-text contrast criterion
findings.question: Does WCAG define any AAA-level success criterion for non-text contrast?
findings.claim: No. SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast exists only at Level AA. The Level AAA criteria grouped under Guideline 1.4 are 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) — which covers TEXT contrast at 7:1, not non-text — plus 1.4.7 Low or No Background Audio, 1.4.8 Visual Presentation, and 1.4.9 Images of Text (No Exception); none of these addresses non-text/UI-component contrast, so WCAG 2.2 has no AAA equivalent of 1.4.11.
findings.quoted_line: How to Meet Non-text Contrast (Level AA)
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 (Success Criterion 1.4.11 heading) and WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference (full 1.4.x criteria/levels list)

findings.question: What is the minimum pointer-target size required by SC 2.5.8?
findings.claim: SC 2.5.8 (Level AA) requires pointer-input targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, subject to five named exceptions (Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, Essential).
findings.quoted_line: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when: Spacing
findings.source_title: WCAG 2.2 — Success Criterion 2.5.8

findings.question: Is the APG a current, actively maintained W3C resource, and what is it primarily used for?
findings.claim: The APG is a live, continuously-revised W3C WAI resource (change history dated back to 2014, maintained by an active APG Task Force via a public mailing list and GitHub), used to teach developers how to build accessibility semantics — design/interaction patterns, keyboard behaviour, ARIA roles/states — into web widgets and components. Unlike WCAG, it is not published as a single dated Recommendation; it is an ungoing, versionless guide.
findings.quoted_line: A history of how the APG has changed, dating back to 2014, including easy access to the detailed commit log is available in the Change History.
findings.source_title: About the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG)

findings.question: Is ISO 24495-1:2023 a real, current, published ISO standard?
findings.claim: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language — Part 1: Governing principles and guidelines is a real, currently Published ISO standard (Edition 1), prepared by Technical Committee ISO/TC 37, published June 2023, 14 pages.
findings.quoted_line: Publication date : 2023-06
findings.source_title: ISO 24495-1:2023 — Plain language, Part 1

findings.question: What are the four core principles of ISO 24495-1:2023, in the standard's own wording?
findings.claim: ISO's own free table-of-contents preview names the four principles, in order, exactly as: Principle 1 relevant ('Readers get what they need'), Principle 2 findable, Principle 3 understandable, Principle 4 usable — confirming the expected wording. The detailed guideline text under each principle (clause 5) is beyond the free preview and paywalled, so only the principle names/order are verified here, not the full guideline content.
findings.quoted_line: 5.1 Guidelines for Principle 1: Readers get what they need (relevant)
findings.source_title: ISO 24495-1:2023(en) — Online Browsing Platform preview

findings.topic: Unicode core specification chapter for Bengali
findings.question: Does the Unicode Standard have a chapter covering Bengali, and does it match U+0980–U+09FF?
findings.claim: The Unicode Standard's core specification, Chapter 12 ('South and Central Asia-I'), covers the Bengali (Bangla) script at code block U+0980–U+09FF.
findings.quoted_line: Bengali: U+0980–U+09FF
findings.source_title: The Unicode Standard, Version 17.0.0 — Core Specification, Chapter 12

findings.question: Does the USE specification exist, and what does it actually specify?
findings.claim: The Universal Shaping Engine (USE) is a real, actively documented OpenType shaping specification (Microsoft Typography, last updated September 2024) that defines syllable clustering, conjunct formation (the 'cjct' feature) and glyph reordering (e.g. 'rphf'/'pref' for reph and pre-base forms) for complex scripts. By its own stated scope, it covers scripts not already handled by a dedicated shaping engine — it is not a universal replacement for every complex-script shaper.
findings.quoted_line: complex scripts included in the Unicode Standard 16.0, but not otherwise supported by a dedicated shaping engine
findings.source_title: Creating and supporting OpenType fonts for the Universal Shaping Engine

findings.topic: Correction: which spec actually governs Bengali shaping
findings.question: Is Bengali actually shaped 'via USE', or does it have its own dedicated shaping specification?
findings.claim: Correction to a common assumption: Microsoft's own typography documentation gives Bengali its own separate, dedicated page ('Developing OpenType Fonts for Bengali Script'), which explicitly invokes 'the Indic shaping engine' — a distinct, older specification from USE. This matches USE's own stated scope (only for scripts without a dedicated shaper). Both specs describe similar mechanics (conjuncts, reph/matra reordering) using shared OpenType feature tags, but they are formally separate documents, so 'Bengali is shaped by USE' is not accurate as a blanket statement per this primary source.
findings.quoted_line: Once the Indic shaping engine has analyzed the cluster as described above, it creates and manages a buffer
findings.source_title: Developing OpenType Fonts for Bengali Script

findings.question: Does CLDR's Bengali (bn) locale default to native Bengali digits (০-৯) or Western digits?
findings.claim: CLDR's root/base 'bn' locale file sets the default numbering system to 'beng' (native Bengali digits ০-৯), not Western digits.
findings.quoted_line: <defaultNumberingSystem>beng</defaultNumberingSystem>
findings.source_title: CLDR common/main/bn.xml

findings.topic: CLDR confirms Bangladesh is Bengali's default territory
findings.question: Does CLDR specifically confirm Bangladesh as Bengali's default/likely territory, with no local override to the digit convention?
findings.claim: CLDR's likelySubtags data maps bare 'bn' to 'bn_Beng_BD' (Bangladesh), and the dedicated bn_BD.xml locale file itself contains no numbering/date overrides at all — it inherits everything, including the native-Bengali-digit default, from the root 'bn' data. This confirms native Bengali digits (০-৯) are CLDR's convention specifically for Bengali as used in Bangladesh.
findings.quoted_line: <likelySubtag from="bn" to="bn_Beng_BD"/>
findings.source_title: CLDR common/supplemental/likelySubtags.xml and common/main/bn_BD.xml

findings.question: Does CLDR treat Bengali-as-used-in-India differently from Bengali-as-used-in-Bangladesh for digits?
findings.claim: Yes — CLDR's 'bn_IN' locale file (Bengali, India) explicitly overrides the default numbering system to 'latn' (Western 0-9 digits), unlike the Bangladesh-default 'beng' (native digits). This is a genuine, sourced country-level distinction within CLDR, not an assumption.
findings.quoted_line: <defaultNumberingSystem>latn</defaultNumberingSystem>
findings.source_title: CLDR common/main/bn_IN.xml

findings.topic: SIL Open Font License current version
findings.question: Is the current OFL version 1.1, and does a version 1.2 exist?
findings.claim: The current and only version of the SIL Open Font License is 1.1, dated 26 February 2007. No version 1.2 exists — the license's own site states it has not changed since 2007, and no '1.2' appears anywhere on the page.
findings.quoted_line: the OFL itself has remained unchanged since 2007
findings.source_title: SIL Open Font License — official site

findings.question: Is openfontlicense.org the canonical URL for the OFL?
findings.claim: Yes — the license's own official text names openfontlicense.org as its own canonical home, in the standard copyright-header template every OFL font is meant to carry.
findings.quoted_line: This license is copied below, and is also available with a FAQ at: https://openfontlicense.org
findings.source_title: SIL Open Font License 1.1 — official text

findings.topic: SIL OFL Reserved Font Name (RFN) restriction
findings.question: What exactly does the Reserved Font Name clause restrict when a font is modified?
findings.claim: A 'Reserved Font Name' is any name the copyright holder declares as such after the copyright statement. A Modified Version of the font may not use that Reserved Font Name without the copyright holder's explicit written permission — but this restriction applies only to the font's primary, user-facing name, not to internal/technical naming.
findings.quoted_line: No Modified Version of the Font Software may use the Reserved Font Name(s) unless explicit written permission is granted by the corresponding Copyright Holder.
findings.source_title: SIL Open Font License 1.1 — official text

findings.topic: Bangla Academy spelling rules — edition identified
findings.question: What edition of প্রমিত বাংলা বানানের নিয়ম (Standard Bengali Spelling Rules) can be verified from a primary/archival copy, and when was it printed?
findings.claim: An archival scan of the actual Bangla Academy publication (not a summary) shows its title page reading "পরিমার্জিত সংস্করণ ২০১২" (Revised Edition 2012), with this particular copy being the "পরিমার্জিত সংস্করণ প্রথম পুনর্মুদ্রণ" (first reprint of the revised edition), dated Magh 1421 of the Bengali calendar / January 2015.
findings.quoted_line: বাংলা একাডেমি প্রমিত বাংলা বানানের নিয়ম (পরিমার্জিত সংস্করণ ২০১২) — পরিমার্জিত সংস্করণ প্রথম পুনর্মুদ্রণ — মাঘ ১৪২১/জানুয়ারি ২০১৫
findings.source_title: বাংলা একাডেমি প্রমিত বাংলা বানানের নিয়ম (Internet Archive item page, viewed directly)
findings.publisher: Internet Archive (hosting a scanned Bangla Academy publication)

findings.topic: Bangla Academy spelling rules — earliest dated copy found
findings.question: Is there an earlier dated edition of the spelling rules accessible, e.g. from an original 1988/1992 edition?
findings.claim: A separate, distinct archive.org item titled "Bangla Academy Pramita Bangla Bananer Niyam" is dated 1992 and self-describes as "Standard Bengali spelling as laid out by the Bangla Academy, Dhaka." This is the earliest dated copy of the document I could directly access and read today; the page itself does not state whether 1992 was the very first edition or already a reprint of an earlier one.
findings.quoted_line: Publication date 1992 ... Standard Bengali spelling as laid out by the Bangla Academy, Dhaka
findings.source_title: Bangla Academy Pramita Bangla Bananer Niyam (Internet Archive item page, viewed directly)
findings.publisher: Internet Archive (hosting a scanned Bangla Academy publication)

findings.topic: Bangla Academy's own website — spelling-rules content
findings.question: Does Bangla Academy's own official website publish the spelling-rules booklet or a page describing its editions?
findings.claim: Bangla Academy's official website (banglaacademy.gov.bd) has a page titled "অভিধান ও বিশ্বকোষ" (Dictionaries and Encyclopaedias) which I loaded directly today; its body contains no actual dictionary or spelling-rules content, only a placeholder string. I found no dedicated page on the official site hosting the রুলস booklet itself or narrating its edition history.
findings.source_title: অভিধান ও বিশ্বকোষ | পাতা | বাংলা একাডেমি

findings.topic: Bangla Academy's own dated statement on spelling debate
findings.question: Has Bangla Academy issued any dated official statement addressing ongoing spelling debate, and does it point to a newer edition of the rules?
findings.claim: A dated notice published on Bangla Academy's own official website on 14 July 2020 states its 'Modern Bengali Dictionary' (আধুনিক বাংলা অভিধান) was first published 1 February 2016 with a first revised/enlarged edition in April 2016, and that alternative spellings from the public debate were folded into that dictionary's revision — but this notice concerns the dictionary, not a new edition of the প্রমিত বাংলা বানানের নিয়ম rules booklet itself, so it does not establish a post-2012 edition of the rules.
findings.quoted_line: 'বাংলা একাডেমি আধুনিক বাংলা অভিধান' প্রথম প্রকাশিত হয় ১লা ফেব্রুয়ারি ২০১৬ সালে... অভিধানটির প্রথম পরিবর্ধিত ও পরিমার্জিত সংস্করণ প্রকাশিত হয় এপ্রিল ২০১৬ সালে।
findings.source_title: বানান বিষয়ক চলমান বিতর্ক নিরসনে বাংলা একাডেমির ভাষ্য (official notice)

findings.topic: Bangladesh Computer Council's own website — keyboard/font standards content
findings.question: Does BCC's official website publish the Bangla keyboard standard or Nikosh font documentation directly?
findings.claim: BCC's official website page titled "স্ট্যান্ডার্ডস উন্নয়ন" (Standards Development), which I loaded directly today, contains no substantive body content — only a placeholder string where the standards documentation would be. I could not locate the BDS 1738 keyboard-standard text or any Nikosh font documentation anywhere on BCC's own site.
findings.source_title: স্ট্যান্ডার্ডস উন্নয়ন | পাতা | বাংলাদেশ কম্পিউটার কাউন্সিল (বিসিসি)

findings.topic: Nikosh font — claimed origin and licence conflict in available sources
findings.question: Does BCC publish/endorse Nikosh as a standard reference font, and under what licence?
findings.claim: Secondary sources disagree on both the body behind Nikosh and its licence. A specialised Bangla web-font catalogue states its designers are named individuals and that the organisation behind it is 'the Election Commission of Bangladesh' (not the Bangladesh Computer Council), releasing it under 'Creative Common License, v3' — attribution required, non-commercial use only, no derivatives — which would contradict the widespread separate claim that Nikosh is freely usable for commercial and government work. Neither claim could be checked against a true primary document (an official licence file or a BCC/Election Commission statement) today, since BCC's own page was empty and no official licence text was located.
findings.source_title: Nikosh | Bangla Web Fonts
findings.publisher: fonts.maateen.me (independent Bangla web-font documentation site, not a government source)

findings.topic: Classification of what each body publishes
findings.question: Does Bangla Academy or Bangladesh Computer Council publish a design system, a brand book, or both, in the sense used for this benchmark?
findings.claim: Bangla Academy's spelling-rules document functions like a 'brand book' for the Bengali language: it is identity/usage governance (correct forms, meaning-bearing conventions) with no code, tokens, or components. BCC's claimed keyboard-layout and reference-font standards would be the nearer analogue to a 'design system' (a technical/engineering specification — a physical key-mapping standard and a reference typeface) but I could not access BCC's own specification content today to confirm its actual form or completeness.
findings.source_title: n/a — structural inference from the two sites examined

could_not_verify.question: Whether Apple maintains any non-public, internal brand governance book (identity/voice/architecture) cannot be verified either way from public sources — only its absence from Apple's public-facing pages was confirmed.

The dedicated Icon Composer sub-page of the HIG (developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/icon-composer) was not independently opened in this session; the Icon Composer findings above are sourced from its treatment on the App Icons overview page, which is a primary source but may not be the most detailed available page on that specific tool.

No official Apple definition/formula for what distinguishes 'clear light' from 'clear dark' or 'tinted light' from 'tinted dark' beyond their listing in the App Icons specifications table was found in the pages read; the underlying rendering logic for each variant was not detailed on the pages retrieved.

Whether any Apple developer-only (Apple ID/NDA-gated) documentation contains numeric animation durations or named easing curves could not be checked, since this research was limited to publicly accessible HIG pages.

Could not access or verify the content of Google's gated internal 'Brand Standards' site (agency-only, requires a Google contact for access), so whether it constitutes a full identity/voice governance brand book beyond the public trademark-permission guidance could not be confirmed.

Did not check whether background/onBackground/surfaceVariant carry a 'deprecated' tag in the older XML/View-based Material Components for Android (non-Compose) documentation — only the current Jetpack Compose Material3 ColorScheme API reference was checked and read.

Could not find a GitHub Releases-based version/date for material-color-utilities beyond its raw commit history, since the repository does not use GitHub's Releases feature ('There aren't any releases here').

Did not directly load the standalone web tool at material.io/theme-builder to confirm it is still functionally live (only its GitHub source, now archived, and its Figma plugin listing, still published, were checked).

Whether Astryx's 170+ components, or the Meta Horizon OS design-system components, are actually used to build Meta's own production consumer apps (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp) or are used only for internal tools and third-party/external adopters — no primary source found either confirming or denying this, so no claim is made about Astryx being 'the design system behind Facebook/Instagram/WhatsApp's own UI.'

The detailed internal criteria and turnaround time of Meta's 'Brand Review' approval process for third-party use of the Meta or product logos — the Brand Resource Center references this process but gates the actual workflow behind an internal Meta contact, so its substance could not be verified from a public primary source.

Whether there is a single dedicated Meta newsroom post explicitly announcing the exact date app-store/marketing copy switched wording from 'from Facebook' (2019 convention) to 'from Meta' (current convention) — the 2021 rename announcement and founder's letter cover the corporate rename narratively, but no primary source pinpointing the exact copy-change date was found.

The explicit business rationale, in Meta's own words, for why Threads is credited to 'Instagram, Inc.' on app stores rather than to 'Meta Platforms, Inc.' or given a 'from Meta' tag — this tiering is an observed structural pattern, not one Meta has explained in a primary source.
